doc.title: Eddie Metz Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, October 3, 2015

chapter: College and the road to jazz
title: Flunking out, William Paterson, the cassette and Basie's call
summary: He flunks out, returns as a music major, transfers to William Paterson, sends a cassette to Grover Mitchell and gets a call from Count Basie.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Yeah. You know, drinking and smoking pot and girls and all that stuff, and I was just happy going to band and playing gigs along the way. And I said hey, this isn’t terrible. Forget those classes. So eventually technically I flunked out of Eastern Michigan. So I laid off a semester and went back on my own dime, I went and found a day job, along with doing the other gigs, and got my own apartment, and went back as a music major, a music education major, taking clarinet and theory and all that stuff. And I got a 4.0. Back then a 4.0 was the highest you could get. I had straight A’s right down the board. And I mailed my report card to my dad. And I said, “dad, I’m thinking of coming to William Paterson College in New Jersey. They have a jazz program there and I really want to be a professional musician.” He was like, “okay. You’ve proved it to me that you really want to do this.” So I moved to New Jersey where my parents had lived. They moved there in the middle of my senior year in high school but I had stayed out there. Another traumatic story but that’s okay. And I’m over it. And went to Eastern as a music major, moved back to New Jersey and went to William Paterson college in Wayne, New Jersey, entered the jazz studies in performance and they accepted me. And I transferred enough academics that I had taken at Eastern and actually passed to transfer in to only take music classes when I went to William Paterson. That was great. That started in 1980. Two years later I was trying to — a friend of mine was playing with Grover Mitchell. He was playing trombone in the Basie band. He had a band that was playing at the Red Parrot in New York City and the Rainbow Room, back and forth, when the Basie band wasn’t on the road. And it was all the Basie guys. So a friend of mine was John Melito, a trumpet player, he’d been in Clark Terry’s last big band. He said, “Eddie, put a cassette together.” A cassette. “We’re having drummer problems. The drummer is terrible.” He said, “just get me a cassette as soon as you can.” So I put it together that night and got it to him. He took it to the gig and gave it to Grover. I didn’t think anything of it, thinking maybe the next time Grover gets his band together after the Basie band’s not on the road, that I
would get that job and stay in school and just do that. And about three months after I did that I got a phone call. It was Labor Day 1982 and it was Count Basie calling me personally.

Yeah. I had all my information on the cassette. And what had happened was Grover was listening to it on the bus and he said, “hey Basie, here, listen to this.” Because Greg Fields was getting ready to leave. Maybe we could check this guy out. I had big band stuff on there. And he said yeah sure. So Basie called me personally. I said, “who is this?” Who’s messing with me, you know? And then I recognized his voice it was like oh my gosh.
